cards.text: Jesus just finished teaching His disciples about money, and He ended with this: "You cannot serve both God and money." The Pharisees, a group of Jewish religious leaders, heard all of it. And friend, the text tells us something about these men that makes this moment REAL awkward.

cards.question: The text describes the Pharisees as lovers of what?
The Pharisees heard Jesus teach that nobody can serve both God and money. They were ___ at Him.

cards.text: Lovers of money scoffing at a talk about money is me scoffing at the smoke alarm while my apron's on FIRE. Jesus tells them, "You are the ones who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts."

cards.question: Jesus goes on to the Pharisees: what is prized among men is ___ before God.

cards.text: Then Jesus says the Law and the Prophets were proclaimed until John, the one who preached a baptism of repentance (Luke 3:3). After John, friend, the preaching changes, and OH, does it change.

cards.question: Since John's time, what does Jesus say is being preached?

answers.text: The gospel of the kingdom of God
A new set of laws for Israel
A call to rebuild the temple

cards.text: And Jesus says everyone is forcing his way into it. Like a bakery door when a fresh batch comes out of the oven: ELBOWS, friend, ELBOWS EVERYWHERE.

cards.question: Jesus says one thing is easier than a single stroke of a pen dropping out of the Law. What is it?

answers.text: A camel through a needle's eye
The sun standing still in the sky

cards.text: Then Jesus speaks plainly about marriage. Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery.

cards.question: Jesus also says that a man who marries a divorced woman does not commit adultery.

cards.text: Then Jesus tells a story about "a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen, who lived each day in joyous splendor." EACH DAY, friend, and I've got ONE apron.
Now at that rich man's gate lies a beggar named Lazarus, covered with sores. Same address, friend. VERY different days.

cards.question: Lazarus is lying at the rich man's gate. What is he longing to be fed with?

answers.text: The crumbs from the rich man's table
Grain left in the nearby fields

cards.question: Even the dogs come and lick the sores of Lazarus the beggar.

cards.text: One day, Lazarus the beggar dies. But he doesn't stay lying at that gate.

cards.question: When Lazarus dies, the angels carry him away. Where do they take him?

cards.text: And the rich man also died and was buried. All that joyous splendor, and he gets half a verse.
In Hades, where he is in torment, he looks up and sees Abraham, Israel's forefather (Luke 1:73), far off, with Lazarus by his side. The rich man cries out that he is in agony in this fire.

cards.question: The rich man cries out to Abraham for mercy. What does he ask for?

answers.text: Lazarus to cool his tongue with water
A place beside Abraham and Lazarus
One more day back on the earth

cards.text: Abraham answers him, and the first word he says is Child.

cards.question: Abraham tells the rich man he received good things in his lifetime and Lazarus received bad things. But now Lazarus is ___ while the rich man is in agony.
Besides all this, Abraham says a great chasm has been fixed between them, so no one can ___ from one side to the other.
Abraham says anyone on his side who wishes to cross over to the rich man can do it.

cards.text: So the rich man begs Abraham to send Lazarus to his father's house. Even down there, he's thinking about home.

cards.question: Why does the rich man want Lazarus sent to his father's house?

answers.text: To pay back his old debts

cards.text: Abraham doesn't send Lazarus anywhere. He says those brothers already have something to listen to.

cards.question: What does Abraham say the rich man's brothers already have?

answers.text: The elders at the city gate

cards.text: No, father Abraham, the rich man says, if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent. That's me arguing with my oven timer: "Trust me, MY plan's better."

cards.question: Abraham says that if someone rises from the dead, that will finally persuade the rich man's brothers.

cards.text: Abraham's last word: if they won't listen to Moses and the Prophets, they won't be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. Those brothers didn't need a bigger sign, friend, because they already had the Word.

findings.problem: No story card sets up Luke 16:17. The baker is asked to guess what Jesus compares a stroke of the pen to, which is guessing the wording of the line. Nothing on earlier cards lets a baker reason toward 'heaven and earth' over the other two.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The wrong answers make the same point as the right one. 'A camel through a needle's eye' is itself a Bible picture of something near impossible (Luke 18:25). 'The sun standing still' is also a picture of something that almost never happens. A baker could argue either one carries the meaning of Luke 16:17, that the Law will never lose a stroke.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: 'Even down there, he's thinking about home' states what the rich man is thinking as fact. Luke 16:27 only says he begs Abraham to send Lazarus to his father's house. The line also leans toward the wrong answer 'To tell his family goodbye' on the next card.

rule.text: Feelings. He can guess at a feeling, marked as his own ("I think," "I bet"). Never as fact.

findings.problem: The bakery-door joke ('ELBOWS EVERYWHERE') pictures 'everyone is forcing his way into it' (Luke 16:16) as an eager, crowding rush. Interpreters disagree on what the phrase means, and the joke quietly settles that question.
findings.question: Can a joke picture a debated phrase in one particular way, or should the comparison stay neutral on what 'forcing his way into it' means? The 'Leave open what the text leaves open' rule lists who, why and how two things connect, but not the meaning of a debated phrase.
